title: Australia won't follow US, other nations in banning Chinese cars from military sites
text: Australia won’t follow US, other nations in banning Chinese cars from military sites The US has specifically banned BYD vehicles from one of its air bases, the latest in a series of bans on Chinese vehicles at sensitive locations, but Australia hasn't announced plans to impose bans of its own. The US has specifically banned BYD vehicles from one of its air bases, the latest in a series of bans on Chinese vehicles at sensitive locations, but Australia hasn't announced plans to impose bans of its own. Concerns over Chinese vehicles surreptitiously recording sensitive military sites have led to bans on vehicle access by other countries, but Australia isn't following suit.\"We ‌obviously ⁠continue to monitor all the safety around our bases in every respect, but we haven't taken that ​step,\" Defence Minister Richard Marles said on Wednesday, as reported by His remarks follow the US announcing a ban on BYD vehicles at its Kadena Air Base, located on Okinawa island in Japan, earlier this month. Brigadier General John Gallemore made the decision “after a thorough, consultative process which determined that these vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission\".Mr Marles said there was no request from the US for Australia to follow suit with a ban of its own. , Poland banned Chinese-manufactured vehicles from entering secured military facilities unless specified recording or connectivity functions were disabled, with military personnel also prohibited from connecting work phones to their infotainment systems. The UK and Czechia have also instituted similar bans.reporting Federal Intelligence Service director Serge Bavaud as saying: \"These cars are smartphones on wheels.The authorities in this country are working with the manufacturers. And the intelligence services can access the data recorded by the cars, for example, conversations\".Concerns over Chinese vehicles being used to spy on sensitive sites received more air time in Australia when the ABC's Four Corners program ran a wide-ranging report onIn addition to demonstrating how certain vehicles could be remotely accessed, albeit once a hacker had physically obtained access, it also put a spotlight on Leapmotor for its use of cameras from Dahua. This Chinese company also supplies building security cameras, but these were banned from Australian Government buildings in 2023 following similar bans in the US and UK over spyware fears.Shadow Minister for Defence James Paterson told Four Corners it’s “extraordinary” that vehicles with these cameras are allowed to drive around government buildings and installations, given the firm has been implicated in human rights abuses and mass surveillance of Uyghur people in China. , arguing its vehicles do use Dahua cameras but are \"independently tested for certification for privacy\", and that the footage obtained from its cameras can only be exported from the vehicle via the dashcam function which requires a USB to be physically inserted in the vehicle.
